prose_changes.old: Basil's own preaching indicted the region's grain-hoarders by name and built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea after the famine of 368 — a genuine, near-unprecedented undertaking, though not, as later legend sometimes claims, the first of its kind anywhere.
prose_changes.new: Basil's own preaching indicted the region's grain-hoarders and moved them to open their stores. After the famine of 368 he built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea. It was a genuine, near-unprecedented undertaking, though not, as later legend sometimes claims, the first of its kind anywhere.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text has Basil name the hoarders. Gregory of Nazianzus (Or. 43, NPNF 2.7) says he 'opened the stores of those who possessed them' by his word; Jackson's prolegomena (NPNF 2.8) say the same. The sentence also made 'preaching' the subject of 'built'.

prose_changes.old: The years were not peaceful throughout: this Christian tradition buried its own martyr, Eupsychius of Caesarea, executed under Julian in 362, and endured a hostile imperial church under Valens that drove Gregory of Nyssa briefly into exile.
prose_changes.new: The years were not peaceful throughout. This Christian tradition buried its own martyr, Eupsychius of Caesarea, executed under Julian in 362. Under Valens, a hostile church party had Gregory of Nyssa deposed, and he lived in exile until 378.
prose_changes.reason: 'Briefly' is not what the sources show and clashes with the entry's own voices text ('exiled under Valens for years'): Basil's letters date the deposition to about 376, and the NPNF 7 headnote dates his return to Valens's death in 378.

prose_changes.old: Damasus's own secretary was Jerome, who carried Rome's claims into the next generation's ascetic-literary circles; the Nicene settlement received at Chalcedon in 451 is the same creed the Cappadocian churches had helped work out a generation earlier.
prose_changes.new: Jerome served as secretary to Damasus of Rome. He had earlier written to Damasus that he kept communion only with 'the chair of Peter'. The creed received at Chalcedon in 451 came from the council of 381, where bishops of the Cappadocian churches took part.
prose_changes.reason: Jerome's letters show the secretaryship and his loyalty to 'the chair of Peter' (Epp. 15, 123), not that he carried Rome's claims into later circles. No vendored text says the Cappadocians helped work out the creed of 381, and 381 is seventy years before Chalcedon, not 'a generation'. Socrates V.8 and CTh 16.1.3 show them at and favored by the council.

prose_changes.old: He would not give it up, and his congregation stayed inside with him — prepared, an eyewitness later wrote, to die with their bishop. It was there, waiting through the night, that Milan's people first sang hymns the way the Eastern churches did, a custom that, by that eyewitness's account, never stopped and spread to churches across the world.
prose_changes.new: He would not give it up, and his congregation stayed inside with him. Augustine, then living in Milan, later wrote that they were 'prepared to die with their bishop'. He also wrote that at this time Milan's people began to sing hymns and psalms in the Eastern way. That custom, he says, lasted and spread to almost all congregations elsewhere.
prose_changes.reason: Augustine was not inside the basilica. Confessions IX.7 says his mother kept watch there, while 'we ... were yet moved by the astonished and disturbed city'. He was a witness in the city, not an eyewitness of the siege, and he does not mention a night.

prose_changes.old: Waiting through the siege night in 386, Ambrose's besieged congregation began singing psalms 'after the manner of the Eastern Church' — and Augustine, who was there, says the custom was 'retained from then till now' and copied by 'almost all' congregations 'throughout the rest of the world.'
prose_changes.new: During the siege of 386, Ambrose's congregation began singing psalms 'after the manner of the Eastern Church'. Augustine, then living in Milan, says the custom was 'retained from then till now'. He adds that 'almost all' congregations 'throughout the rest of the world' copied it.
prose_changes.reason: Same correction as the longDescription: Confessions IX.7 places Augustine in the city, not in the basilica, and mentions no night. The four quoted phrases are unchanged and appear verbatim in the NPNF 1.1 text.

prose_changes.old: Historical-literal exegesis, set against Alexandria's allegorical method; Theodore of Mopsuestia's own contested status is noted here on the record.
prose_changes.new: Historical-literal exegesis, set against Alexandria's allegorical method, though scholars dispute how sharp the contrast was. Theodore of Mopsuestia wrote against Origen, was condemned in 553, and was defended by the Church of the East as its 'Interpreter'.
prose_changes.reason: 'Noted here on the record' is cataloguing language. The project's Antiochene world already tags the broad literal-versus-allegorical contrast Contested (aec_Superseded_Claims 3.3). Theodore's book against Origen (Facundus III.6), the 553 canon and the 585 synod's defense are all in vendored texts.

prose_changes.old: They were quarried for medieval preaching, printed early and often in the Reformation era — Reformed and Lutheran preachers alike claimed him as an ancestor of expository preaching.
prose_changes.new: Reformation writers quoted him too. Calvin prized his saying that humility is 'the foundation of our philosophy', though he thought Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. The Augsburg Confession of 1530 cited him on how the early church shared Communion.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source shows medieval quarrying, early printing, or a Reformed or Lutheran claim of ancestry for expository preaching. Calvin's Institutes (II.2.4, II.2.11) and the Augsburg Confession (XXIV) show the use that is documented.

prose_changes.old: The Antiochene way of reading, insisting that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it, is the ancestor of the historical-grammatical method that later Western biblical scholarship made standard.
prose_changes.new: The Antiochene way of reading insisted that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it. Later Western biblical scholarship made a similar historical-grammatical method standard, though no direct line between the two has been traced.
prose_changes.reason: 'Is the ancestor of' is a genealogical claim no vendored or repo-cited source supports. The likeness of method is fair to state; the descent is not.

prose_changes.old: It worshipped in Syriac, thought in the exegetical idiom it shared with Edessa and Antioch, and was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
prose_changes.new: It worshipped in Syriac and shared the learning of Edessa. Persian students there read Theodore of Mopsuestia's commentaries once they were put into Syriac, and the church's later teachers made his Antiochene way of reading their own. And it was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text shows the Persian church before 451 sharing Antioch's exegetical idiom. Barhadbeshabba (Cause of the Schools) shows Persian students at Edessa studying Theodore in Syriac; the synod of 585 shows the later church adopting him.

prose_changes.old: In 384 Blaesilla took up the severe fasting Jerome taught and was dead within four months; at her funeral a Roman crowd shouted for the monks to be thrown in the Tiber, and Jerome's own consolation letter to the grieving Paula admits he wept writing it.
prose_changes.new: In 384 Blaesilla took up the severe fasting Jerome taught and was dead within four months. At her funeral, Jerome reports, people in the crowd muttered that the monks should be stoned or thrown in the Tiber. His consolation letter to the grieving Paula admits that the whole letter was written in tears.
prose_changes.reason: Jerome's Letter 39 (npnf206 8109-8115) says the words were 'whispers ... audible in the crowd', not shouts, and asks why the monks are not stoned or thrown in the Tiber. He writes that 'this entire letter is written in tears' (7820-7821). Long sentence also split.

prose_changes.old: Eustochium sent Rome a full account of it, and the pope who answered her praised the community for one thing above all — that they had never named the man behind it.
prose_changes.new: Eustochium and her niece Paula sent Rome an account of it. Pope Innocent, writing to the bishop of Jerusalem, praised the "wonderful clemency" with which they had left the attacker's name untold.
prose_changes.reason: Innocent's praise is in his letter to John of Jerusalem, not in an answer to Eustochium (Jerome, Ep. 137; npnf206 28467-28474), and the letter names both women. 'Above all' is not in the source.

prose_changes.old: Its rise was not immediate or uncontested: Augustine himself never accepted it, writing after Jerome's death that even though the Jews themselves granted his Hebrew work faithful, 'the churches of Christ judge that no one should be preferred to the authority' of the Seventy translators — and the older Greek-based Latin version he defended stayed in real use for generations afterward.
prose_changes.new: Its rise was not immediate or uncontested. Augustine quoted Jerome's Hebrew version at times, but he never gave it the old version's authority. Writing after Jerome's death, he granted that even the Jews judged the work faithful, yet 'the churches of Christ judge that no one should be preferred to the authority' of the Seventy translators. In the 590s, Pope Gregory the Great still drew on both the new Latin version and the old.
prose_changes.reason: 'Never accepted it' is contradicted by De doctrina christiana IV.7.15, where Augustine follows 'the translation made from the Hebrew into Latin by the presbyter Jerome' (npnf102 54117-54119). 'Stayed in real use for generations' now rests on Gregory's Moralia preface: 'I take now the new and now the old' (gregory-great_moralia-in-job-books-i-x_bliss1844.txt 1006-1008). The 'Augustine never accepted it' wording is replaced; the City of God quote is kept verbatim (npnf102 36741-36742). Split from one 70-word sentence.

prose_changes.old: Its principle mattered as much as its content: Jerome's insistence on going back to the Hebrew rather than resting on the Greek is the ancestor of every later "back to the sources" movement, including the Renaissance and Reformation scholarship that eventually turned on the Vulgate itself.
prose_changes.new: Its principle mattered as much as its content. Jerome insisted on going back to the Hebrew rather than resting on the Greek. Later scholars of the Renaissance and Reformation made the same kind of appeal to the original languages, and in the end they turned it on the Vulgate itself.
prose_changes.reason: 'The ancestor of every later back-to-the-sources movement' is a lineage claim no vendored or repo-cited source makes. The rewrite keeps the comparison and drops the descent. A repo-cited study would let the stronger claim return.

prose_changes.old: Folded into the Imperial-Juridical tradition as one of its three phases
prose_changes.new: Ambrose's Milan was the seat of the western court, and its bishop argued with that court in public. His claim that the emperor is within the church, not above it, is one of the three answers told in Imperial and Juridical Christianity.
prose_changes.reason: The old line was cataloguing language ('folded into ... as one of its phases') and miscounted the imperial entry's 'three answers' as 'phases'. Replaced with the relationship itself, now carried by ambrosian-milan-standalone--imperial-juridical-christianity. The quote 'within the Church, not above it' is Ambrose's own (npnf210 42663-42664).

prose_changes.old: His confrontation with Theodosius became a standing precedent, cited for more than a millennium, that a Christian ruler stands under the church's discipline rather than above it.
prose_changes.new: Within two generations, a Greek historian, Theodoret, was retelling his stand against Theodosius. Ambrose had already stated the rule himself. A Christian ruler stands within the church, not above it.
prose_changes.reason: 'Cited for more than a millennium' has no vendored or repo-cited support. Theodoret's Church History (c. 450) retells the episode (npnf203 16499-16503), and the rule is Ambrose's own words from 386 (npnf210 42663-42664).

prose_changes.old: Adjacent to ambrosian-milan-standalone in region and generation, and to hieronymian-ascetic-literary in personnel - Jerome and Rufinus were formed here together and quarreled elsewhere. Its transmission relation to alexandria-catechetical is the consequential one: Rufinus is why Origen survives in Latin at all.
prose_changes.new: Next to Ambrose's Milan in place and time, and tied to Jerome's circle at Bethlehem by its people. Jerome and Rufinus were formed here together and later quarreled. Its tie to the Alexandrian school matters most. Rufinus's translations are why much of Origen survives in Latin at all.
prose_changes.reason: Three raw movement ids printed to readers, replaced by plain names; internal 'transmission relation' removed. 'Quarreled elsewhere' is wrong in part (Rufinus wrote his Apology at Aquileia, per the npnf203 heading at 46237). 'Why Origen survives in Latin at all' overstated: Gennadius notes Jerome translated some of Origen too (npnf203 42480-42481), so 'much of'.

prose_changes.old: In 381 Ambrose came up from Milan and presided over a council at Aquileia that deposed the last two Homoian bishops of the Danube provinces.
prose_changes.new: In 381 Ambrose came up from Milan to a council at Aquileia. The record names the city's own bishop, Valerian, first. Ambrose led the questioning. The council condemned two Homoian bishops of the Danube provinces, Palladius and Secundianus.
prose_changes.reason: Era-2 open item. The Acts do not say Ambrose presided: they list Valerian first and show Ambrose leading the questioning (Mansi 3, 59746-59747, 60735-60738). 'The last two' is contradicted by the vendored Auxentius of Durostorum edition: Kauffmann, 'Auxentius ... war bischof von Dorostorum (Silistria) in Moesia inferior' (auxentius-durostorum...kauffmann1899.txt 3397), a Homoian bishop on the Danube after 381.

prose_changes.old: It is the earliest evidence that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
prose_changes.new: Rufinus's own words show that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
prose_changes.reason: 'The earliest evidence' is not shown by any vendored or repo-cited source. Rufinus himself says that 'in different Churches some additions are found' (npnf203 56728-56729), which supports the plainer claim.

prose_changes.old: It is the earliest evidence that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
prose_changes.new: Rufinus's own words show that the Western churches did not all say the same words at the font.
prose_changes.reason: Same sentence and same reason as the longDescription change.

prose_changes.old: The descent into hell, which every later version carries, is first attested here - Rufinus notes that the Roman creed lacks it - and it entered the received Western text from the provincial creeds rather than from Rome.
prose_changes.new: The descent into hell, which every later version carries, is first attested in a Western baptismal creed here. Rufinus notes that the Roman creed lacks it, though a creed drawn up at Sirmium in 359 already had a form of it. It entered the received Western text from the provincial creeds rather than from Rome.
prose_changes.reason: 'First attested here' is contradicted by the Dated Creed of Sirmium (359), which has 'descended into the lower parts of the earth' (Socrates HE II.37, npnf202 8562-8563). Narrowed to Western baptismal creeds.

prose_changes.old: Rufinus' commentary is also the earliest systematic exposition of a creed in Latin and the model for the genre.
prose_changes.new: Rufinus' commentary is also one of the first full explanations of a creed in Latin. Other writers had explained it briefly before him, he says. A century later, Gennadius judged it so good that other explanations counted for nothing beside it.
prose_changes.reason: 'The earliest systematic exposition' is contradicted by Rufinus: 'some eminent writers have published treatises on these matters' (npnf203 56634-56636). 'The model for the genre' is replaced by Gennadius's judgment (npnf203 42482-42484).

prose_changes.old: Ambrose of Milan - who came up the road in 381 to preside over the council that finished the Homoian bishops of Illyricum
prose_changes.new: Ambrose of Milan - who came up the road in 381 to the council that condemned two Homoian bishops of Illyricum, and led its questioning
prose_changes.reason: Era-2 open item ('presided' appears here too). The Acts show Ambrose leading the questioning, not presiding; 'finished the Homoian bishops' is contradicted by Auxentius of Durostorum (see the longDescription change).

prose_changes.old: The other half of fourth-century Gaul, and deliberately separate from gallic-monastic-ascetic-christianity: an episcopate resisting an imperial creed, not a monastery. The two touch at one point that matters - Martin of Tours was Hilary's disciple, and the monastic world grows out of the ground this one defended.
prose_changes.new: The other half of fourth-century Gaul, beside Gallic monastic Christianity. This was an episcopate resisting an imperial creed, not a monastery. The two touch at one point that matters. Martin of Tours was Hilary's disciple, and the monastic world grew up in the Gaul these bishops defended.
prose_changes.reason: Raw movement id printed to readers, replaced by its plain name; 'deliberately separate from' was cataloguing commentary. 'Grows out of the ground' read as descent; the existing link is 'influenced' (Sulpicius, Vita Martini 5-7).

prose_changes.old: Hilary's De Trinitate gave Latin theology its first full-scale treatment of the doctrine, and Augustine, who did the second, worked with it in view. The Gallic repudiation of Ariminum at Paris also mattered practically: it kept the western provinces out of the Homoian settlement that the Gothic kingdoms would later inherit, so that the Frankish conversion two centuries on was to a Nicene church rather than an Arian one. And Hilary ordained Martin, which makes this episcopate the immediate ancestor of the monastic Gaul that grew up beside it.
prose_changes.new: Hilary's De Trinitate gave Latin theology its first full-scale treatment of the doctrine. Augustine, who wrote the second, quotes it by name. The Gallic rejection of Ariminum also mattered in practice. Sulpicius Severus, writing some forty years later, says Hilary alone freed Gaul from heresy. Two centuries on, Gregory of Tours told how a light from Hilary's church at Poitiers led the Frankish king Clovis against the Arian Goths. Gregory saw it as Hilary's help against the heretics he had fought. And Hilary ordained Martin, which ties these bishops to the monastic Gaul that grew up beside them.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims fixed. (1) 'Kept the western provinces out of the Homoian settlement that the Gothic kingdoms would later inherit, so that the Frankish conversion ... was to a Nicene church' is a causal chain no source gives; replaced by what Sulpicius (Chron. II.45, npnf211 11433-11434) and Gregory of Tours (HF II.37, III preface; dalton1927 3710-3713, 4100-4102) say. (2) 'Immediate ancestor of the monastic Gaul' read as descent; the link is 'influenced'. (3) 'Worked with it in view' made concrete: Augustine names Hilary's book (npnf103 9190-9191).

prose_changes.old: Rival-sibling of the Latin pastoral congregational tradition it split from over the same persecution; its refusal of any imperial standing to judge the church is the mirror image of Imperial and Juridical Christianity's own church-state alliance, and its once-for-all rebaptism is the opposite answer Cappadocian Christianity gave to the same question of how someone from the other side comes back in.
prose_changes.new: The rival of the Latin pastoral church of Carthage and Hippo, from which it split over the same persecution. Its bishop Donatus asked what the emperor had to do with the church, the reverse of the church-state alliance of Imperial and Juridical Christianity. And it baptized again those who came over from the other side. Basil of Caesarea, by contrast, wrote that the old rule was to accept the baptism of schismatics.
prose_changes.reason: The Cappadocian comparison is not a relationship and was overstated: Basil's Letter 188, canon 1 (npnf208 34825-34826) reports the ancients' rule to 'admit that of schismatics', while noting that Cyprian and Firmilian had rejected it; 'the opposite answer' is narrowed to what he wrote. 'Rival-sibling' and 'once-for-all rebaptism' are replaced with plain words; the imperial clause now rests on Donatus's own question (Optatus III, line 1904). The 'split' is carried by the new broke-with link.

prose_changes.old: A rural movement called the circumcellions is attested in this same period by an imperial fine — a real, legally distinct group — though almost everything claimed about what they actually did survives only in the writing of opponents who had reason to make them look like a mob.
prose_changes.new: A rural movement called the circumcellions appears in Optatus's account of these same years. An imperial law of 412 fined them as a class of their own, so they were a real, legally distinct group. But almost everything said about what they did comes from opponents who had reason to make them look like a mob.
prose_changes.reason: The imperial fine is the law of 30 January 412 (Codex Theodosianus 16.5.52, 'circumcelliones argenti pondo decem', codex-theodosianus_latinlibrary.txt line 7186), not 'this same period' as 347. Optatus names them in the 340s (Latin, Ziwsa CSEL 26 line 3686).

prose_changes.old: The communion survived under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for a further century and a half, still contested and still legislated against — the last word any surviving record has on it is a set of letters Pope Gregory the Great wrote in the 590s, pressing for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism in Numidia.
prose_changes.new: The sources say little about the communion under the Vandals, but it was still there under Byzantine rule. In 535 Justinian's law for Africa barred Donatists from holding services. The last surviving word on it comes from Pope Gregory the Great. His letters of the 590s pressed for an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism in Numidia.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored text shows Donatists under Vandal rule or Vandal laws against them; Victor of Vita names them only as the target of the old imperial laws Huneric turned on the Catholics (Historia III, Petschenig line 7149). The Byzantine legislation is documented (Novel 37, link byzantine-imperial-church-justinianic--donatism). The sentence also ran past 50 words.

prose_changes.old: Its two-party contest with the rival Catholic church did not end with the Roman empire that had tried to settle it: Vandal and then Byzantine rulers inherited the same divided towns for another century and a half, the dispute still live enough that a sixth-century pope found it worth four letters of his own.
prose_changes.new: Its contest with the rival Catholic church did not end with the Roman empire that had tried to settle it. A century later, Byzantine emperors were still issuing laws against it. And in the 590s the dispute was live enough that Pope Gregory the Great wrote about it in at least eight letters.
prose_changes.reason: 'Four letters' undercounts: the vendored NPNF selection alone has Gregory naming the Donatists in Register I.74, I.77, II.48, IV (to Pantaleo; to Victor and Columbus), VI.37, VI.63 and VI.65 (npnf212). The Vandal half is not documented (see the longDescription change).

prose_changes.old: a bishop named Marculus was seized, paraded through several towns, and thrown from a cliff called Novapetra, and this communion has kept his name, and the names of others killed with him, read aloud at their graves every year since.
prose_changes.new: a bishop named Marculus was seized, paraded through several towns, and thrown from a cliff called Novapetra. His church honored him and others killed with him as martyrs, and its own account of his death survives.
prose_changes.reason: 'Every year since' cannot be true of a communion that no longer exists, and no vendored text shows the annual reading. What is documented: the Donatists held those killed as martyrs (Augustine, quoted in the PL 8 notes, monumenta-vetera-donatistarum_migne-pl8.txt lines 776-779, 'Ecce Marculus de petra praecipitatus est'), and the Passio Marculi survives (same file, from line 874). The cliff name and the parade are left as they were; the OCR of the Passio is too damaged for me to confirm either.

prose_changes.old: Descended from Egyptian desert monasticism through Cassian, who had lived among the Egyptian monks before founding his houses at Marseilles; the seedbed of the Merovingian Gallic church that follows it, and - through Lérins and Tours - of Irish monasticism.
prose_changes.new: Drew on Egyptian desert monasticism through Cassian, who had lived among the Egyptian monks before founding his houses at Marseilles. It fed the Merovingian Gallic church that follows it. One eighth-century Irish account also traces a line from Cassian and Lérins to Irish monasticism.
prose_changes.reason: 'Descended from' claims more than the influenced link shows, and Martin's monasticism began before Cassian reached Gaul. The Irish link is Inferential-Thin and rests on one tract naming Cassian and Lérins; no listed source names Tours.

prose_changes.old: His supporters responded by making him bishop of Ávila; his opponents accused him of Manichaeism and sorcery and carried the case to the imperial court.
prose_changes.new: His supporters responded by making him bishop of Ávila. He went to Rome and Milan to clear himself, and was turned away by both bishops, Ambrose of Milan among them. His opponents called his teaching the heresy of the Gnostics, accused him of sorcery, and carried the case to the imperial court. Later churchmen likened it to Manichaeism.
prose_changes.reason: The only vendored contemporary account (Sulpicius, Chron. II.46-50) calls the teaching 'the heresy of the Gnostics' and says he was believed to practise magic; the Manichaean charge at the trial is not in a vendored text. The likening is documented later: Leo, Ep. 15 (447), 'they agree with the Manichaeans' (npnf212 3476) and Braga I (561), 'sicut Manicheus et Priscillianus dixerunt' (Bruns line 2510). The Rome-Milan sentence carries the one vendored witness to Ambrose (Chron. II.48), replacing the unsupported claim in prose change 7.

prose_changes.old: It shocked people at the time: Martin of Tours and Ambrose of Milan both objected to churchmen taking a doctrinal quarrel to an executioner, and the bishops who had pressed the charges were disgraced for it.
prose_changes.new: It shocked people at the time. Martin of Tours had begged the emperor not to shed the blood of the accused. A secular ruler, he said, had no place judging a church case. The bishops who had pressed the charges were disgraced for it.
prose_changes.reason: Martin's protest is documented (Chron. II.50, npnf211 11652-11660). Ambrose's objection to the execution is in his Letter 24, which is not vendored (in wants); the vendored evidence on Ambrose is his earlier refusal, now in prose change 6. The disgrace is documented (Chron. II.51: Ithacius 'thrust out of the episcopate', Ydacius resigned).

prose_changes.old: His opponents accused him of Manichaeism and sorcery and carried the case to the imperial court, and around 385 the usurping emperor Magnus Maximus had him and several companions tried and executed at Trier, apparently the first time a Christian state put Christians to death over belief.
prose_changes.new: His opponents called it the heresy of the Gnostics, accused him of sorcery, and carried the case to the imperial court. Around 385 the usurping emperor Magnus Maximus had him and several companions tried and executed at Trier. It was apparently the first time a Christian state put Christians to death over belief.
prose_changes.reason: Same evidence as prose change 6 on the charges; the sentence also ran past 50 words.

prose_changes.old: Martin of Tours and Ambrose of Milan both objected to churchmen taking a doctrinal quarrel to an executioner.
prose_changes.new: Martin of Tours objected to churchmen taking a doctrinal quarrel to an executioner, and begged the emperor to spare the accused.
prose_changes.reason: Same evidence as prose change 7: Martin's protest is vendored, Ambrose's is not.

prose_changes.new: The Homoians — from the Greek homoios, "like" — taught that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures. They refused to go further and call him of one being with the Father, because Scripture never used the word and no council should force it on anyone. prose_changes.reason: Split a 70-word sentence. The Homoian side's own words now carry the claim: Auxentius 48 (Kauffmann 1899, lines 15174-15176, the Son 'like' the Father 'secundum diuinas scribturas') and Maximinus's commentary (line 14834, 'constat ergo Arrium episcopos secutum fuisse, non episcopos Arrium'). prose_changes.new: The Goths became Christians in this form, and the Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards held it too. Jordanes, a sixth-century historian of the Goths, says they passed it on to "all people of their speech." Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene. The Visigoths of Spain went over to the Nicene creed at Toledo in 589, and the Lombards of Italy were the last to follow, two generations later.
prose_changes.reason: 'Through that mission' made Ulfila's own mission the cause of the Vandal, Burgundian and Lombard conversions; no vendored text says so. Socrates IV.33 credits Valens and Fritigern for the Goths, and Jordanes 25.133 (lines 1655-1659) says the Visigoths spread it to the Ostrogoths, Gepids and 'all people of their speech'. Each people's Homoian faith is attested: Vandals (Victor of Vita, 1605 trans., line 2), Burgundians (Gregory of Tours, Brehaut 1916, line 2102), Lombards (Paul the Deacon IV.42, lines 9051-9053, Rothari still Arian, d. 652). prose_changes.old: The clauses most Christians recite each week were sharpened precisely to close the space this tradition tried to hold open.
prose_changes.new: In 381 the Council of Constantinople confirmed the faith of Nicaea, which calls the Son of one being with the Father. In the same canon it condemned the Homoians by name, as "the Arians or Eudoxians."
prose_changes.reason: The creed's key clause dates from 325, before the Homoian party formed (359-360), so 'sharpened precisely' against them is not right. What is documented: Constantinople 381, canon 1, confirms the Nicene faith and anathematizes 'the Arians or Eudoxians' (npnf214, lines 13971-13976, 13985-13987).

prose_changes.old: The radical wing of the fourth-century Arian controversy, and a different party from the Homoians it is usually filed with - the two split at Constantinople in 360.
prose_changes.new: The radical wing of the fourth-century Arian controversy, and a different party from the Homoians it is usually filed with. The break began at Constantinople in 360, when a Homoian council deposed Aetius.
prose_changes.reason: The sources do not put the whole split in 360. The Homoian council of 360 deposed Aetius (Sozomen IV.24; its own letter in Theodoret II.24), but Eunomius stayed with Eudoxius for a time (Theodoret II.25); Socrates IV.13 and Philostorgius IX.4 put the final break under Valens.

prose_changes.old: The party split from the Homoians at Constantinople in the same year, when the Homoian creed was imposed and Aetius exiled - which is why filing the two together misreads the controversy.
prose_changes.new: The break with the Homoians began at Constantinople in the same year, when their council confirmed the Homoian creed and deposed Aetius. Within a few years Eunomius and Aetius had broken away entirely, so filing the two parties together misreads the controversy.
prose_changes.reason: As the summary: 360 is the start of the break, not all of it. Theodoret II.25 dates Eunomius's own sect to after his flight from Cyzicus (c. 361); Socrates IV.13 and Philostorgius IX.4 to Valens's reign. 'Within a few years' covers both.

prose_changes.new: The controversy also shaped the next century. At Ephesus in 431 the bishops heard Cyril's letter saying the Word took flesh "animated by a rational soul." At Chalcedon in 451 they defined Christ as truly man, with a rational soul and a body.
